case_study_insert.main_stem: Summit Trail Guides (STG) is a private limited company in the outdoor recreation and guided tourism sector, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2011 by Maren Torto, the business operates with a flat structure with democratic leadership. STG plans to invest $520,000 in a new automated trail-mapping centre with solar-powered signage, financed by a $300,000 six-year bank loan and retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $52, and currently produces 20,000 units a year. STG faces an operational problem: a growing number of customers report cancelled trips due to weather delays, and staff have become careless in packing guide bags, causing trail litter.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: STG completed 1,200 guided trips, with 96% of trips arriving on time, a customer satisfaction score of 4.6 out of 5, and complaints about trail litter fell from 12 to 3 this quarter. Average processing time for trip bookings is 1.8 days.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Summit Trail Guides for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.8% to 4.6%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $14.50 to $15.30 per hour from January 2027. (3) Food-price inflation is running at 7.0%, and consumer spending on adventure and travel goods grew 2.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: STG is financing its $520,000 trail-mapping centre with a $300,000 six-year bank loan + retained profit. Explain two advantages for STG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Retained profit has no interest repayments or bank charges, which protects STG's weekly cash flow — every dollar not paid as interest on the $300,000 loan is available to absorb the effect of cancelled trips caused by weather delays. Point 2: Financing the $520,000 trail-mapping centre with retained profit means there is no external lender condition on how the centre is run or expanded, so STG keeps full control of the capital and equity.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Summit Trail Guides and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: STG is launching its new trail-mapping centre and has the option of a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should STG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would reach millions of potential buyers very quickly and build strong brand awareness for the new trail-mapping centre. However, airtime and production costs are extremely high, and much of the audience would not be outdoor-trip buyers, so STG could not justify the spend against the $520,000 expansion funded by a six-year bank loan.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper than TV, reaches the area where trips originate, and suits time-sensitive messages such as new product launches. Its limitation is narrow reach — the centre supplies trips across the whole region, so local listeners alone cannot generate the volume needed for the 20,000-unit output target.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with outdoor influencers targets the audience that travels for adventure, with measurable engagement, and matches the new centre's image. Cost per reached customer is low, and it lets STG tell its 96%-on-time delivery story.

Recommendation: STG should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise audience, costs far less than TV, and builds the trip brand — TV is rejected as unaffordable for a $520,000 bank-loan-funded expansion, and radio is rejected as too narrow for the region-wide trip market.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of Summit Trail Guides with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of STG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: STG's customers report cancelled trips due to weather delays, and staff have become careless in packing guide bags. Explain two benefits for STG of using flat structure with democratic leadership to improve motivation in its guide team.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 28 guides a genuine voice in how trips are organised and how the trail-mapping centre is run — staff who help set routines attend more reliably, which directly reduces the number of cancelled trips that weather delays already cause. Point 2: Involving staff in decisions improves the quality of packing — they flag packing errors early, cutting trail litter (currently down from 12 to 3) and keeping the business on schedule for trips.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to STG's weather-delay cancellations and trail litter.

questions.question_text: STG wants to reduce the number of weather-related cancellations. Consider a mobile-app booking system or a redesigned online booking form. Which should STG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Mobile-app booking system: An app can send push notifications about weather delays, allow instant rebooking and collect payment upfront — reducing the number of cancelled trips and the cash-flow disruption they cause. Its downside is development and ongoing costs, which STG could fund from the $520,000 centre budget.

Redesigned online booking form: A better form reduces human error and offers an alternative-date option, but it still depends on customers visiting the form in time, so the reduction in cancellations is only modest.

Decision: STG should choose the mobile-app booking system — it reduces cancellations directly and can be funded from the centre budget. The redesigned online booking form is rejected as too slow to respond to weather delays.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the booking methods in the context of STG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of STG with a well-justified decision covering cancellation reduction and cost.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how STG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($52 − $22) = $360,000 ÷ $30 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $52 − $22 = $30. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways STG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 12,000-unit break-even output with the 20,000 units produced — the margin of safety is 8,000 units, so the centre is profitable on average and the risk of demand dropping below break-even is visible early.
2. Use the $30 contribution per unit to model price changes: a 5% cut to $49.40 would cut contribution to $27.40, so managers would need to check that extra volume covers the $360,000 fixed costs (around 13,139 units at $27.40).
3. Average total cost is about $40 per unit (360,000 ÷ 20,000 + $22 = $18 + $22) against the $52 selling price — a strong margin to absorb weather-related cancellations.
4. Labour productivity of about 714 units per worker (20,000 ÷ 28) helps check the packing care behind the trail litter and decides whether more training is needed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 8,000 units against the 20,000-unit output; discount modelling to $49.40 cutting contribution to $27.40; average total cost benchmarking at $40 per unit against the $52 selling price; and labour productivity of about 714 units per worker to check the trail-litter issue.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate STG's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has STG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 32.5%
ROCE 2024 = 25.0%
ROCE 2025 = 26.0%

Detailed workings:
2024: revenue 500, cost of sales 300, gross profit 200; 2025: revenue 600, cost of sales 330, gross profit 270. OP is 150 in 2024 and 195 in 2025; capital employed is 600 and 750.

Evaluation: Margins have improved — the gross profit margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0% and the profit margin from 30.0% to 32.5%, so both the absolute profit and the efficiency of STG's operations are stronger year on year. OP rose from $150,000 to $195,000 and ROCE from 25.0% to 26.0% as the new centre investment began to generate returns.

Conclusion: STG's financial position has improved — margins, profit and return on capital employed are all higher year on year, so the expansion appears well funded and the business is becoming more efficient.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin and profit margin for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of margin and ROCE trends and a justified conclusion on whether STG's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for STG of introducing eco-packaging for its guided tour and adventure equipment.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-packaging matches customer values — the Operations Report shows 96% of trips arriving on time and trail litter falling from 12 to 3 — so STG can position itself as sustainable without sacrificing reliability, and customers who check packaging can choose STG confidently.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials can add $1–$2 per trip to the $22 variable cost, lowering the $30 contribution per trip and meaning STG may need higher trip volumes to cover the $360,000 fixed costs if the price elasticity of trip bookings is weak.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to STG's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.6%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase to $15.30 and the 7.0% food-price inflation will affect STG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.8% to 4.6%): If STG's $300,000 six-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by about 0.8% of the loan = $2,400 a year — small next to STG's $360,000 fixed costs, so STG should ask for a fixed rate or fixed-price loan terms on the new centre.

Minimum wage rise (5.2% from $14.50 to $15.30): The insert does not state STG's base pay or hours worked, so no exact annual figure can be invented; the judgement is that the whole payroll rises while STG's output is capped at 20,000 units and the new centre still needs to service the $300,000 loan.

Food-price inflation (7.0%): At $22 per unit, 7.0% would add up to $1.54 a trip, or between $20,000 and $40,000 a year at 20,000 trips if fully passed to variable cost, cutting the $30 contribution toward about $28.50. STG can partly offset via higher trip prices, but the operating cost risk is real.

Conclusion: The 7.0% food-price inflation has the greatest impact on STG — it applies on all 20,000 units produced and directly erodes the $30 contribution per trip, whereas the interest rise is small relative to fixed costs and the wage-rise magnitude is uncertain but spread across the payroll.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to Summit Trail Guides.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on STG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of STG with a well-justified judgment that the 7.0% food-price inflation has the greatest impact.
